readFirst.title: What was analyzed
readFirst.body: 606 classified written responses from the Zone 5B and Zone 4A sections of the public survey export.

readFirst.title: Main takeaway
readFirst.body: Against-as-written responses are the largest category overall: 427 responses (70.5%).

readFirst.title: Biggest topic signal
readFirst.body: Parking is the most frequent provisional tag (163 tag assignments). Topic tags are not vote totals.

readFirst.title: Uncertainty to review
readFirst.body: 149 classifications are medium or low confidence; 185 rows are in the broader review queue.

readFirst.title: Best next read
readFirst.body: Use the concern-to-response matrix and glossary before interpreting the charts as decision evidence.

zoneComparison.title: Both zones have majority opposition as written
zoneComparison.summary: Zone 4A is 73.6% against and Zone 5B is 67.3% against.

zoneComparison.title: Zone 4A has more against responses
zoneComparison.summary: The against share is 6.3 percentage points higher in Zone 4A (73.6%) than Zone 5B (67.3%).

zoneComparison.title: Zone 5B is still majority against, but has a larger in-favor share
zoneComparison.summary: Zone 5B remains 67.3% against as written, while its in-favor share is 6.9 percentage points higher than Zone 4A (27.4% vs. 20.5%).

decisionFaq.question: What is the main takeaway?
decisionFaq.answer: Against-as-written responses are the largest category overall: 427 of 606 responses (70.5%).

decisionFaq.question: How different are Zone 4A and Zone 5B?
decisionFaq.answer: Zone 4A has a higher against share (73.6%) than Zone 5B (67.3%). Zone 5B has a higher in-favor share (27.4%) than Zone 4A (20.5%).

decisionFaq.question: What are people worried about?
decisionFaq.answer: The recurring provisional topics include parking, traffic and safety, building height, density, neighborhood character, affordability, transit assumptions, green space, infrastructure, and process or trust.

decisionFaq.question: Are supporters supporting everything?
decisionFaq.answer: Not necessarily. Use the conditional and mixed-response review set to find places where respondents may support housing goals while objecting to specific proposal details.

decisionFaq.question: How reliable is this classification?
decisionFaq.answer: The readout is provisional. 149 classifications are medium or low confidence, and 185 rows are in the review queue because they need review or are mixed/conditional.

decisionFaq.question: Does this prove what all residents think?
decisionFaq.answer: No. It summarizes written responses from the analyzed survey sections. It is not a statistically weighted poll, a referendum, or a policy recommendation.

whatWouldChangeMinds.summary: Rows flagged as mixed, neutral, or conditional are the best starting point for understanding which amendments, safeguards, or evidence could address concerns.
discussionPrompts: Would clearer parking management, loading, or spillover protections reduce opposition?
Would height, massing, setbacks, or transition standards address scale concerns?
Would affordability requirements, duration, and enforcement details make benefits more credible?
Would traffic, school, stormwater, and infrastructure evidence answer capacity concerns?
Would a phased approach or additional public review points improve trust in the process?

confidenceExplainer.summary: Confidence describes how directly a classification follows from the available rationale. It is a review signal, not a judgment about whether a respondent is correct.

levels.meaning: The rationale points clearly to against, neutral, or in-favor as written.
The rationale is mostly clear but may include mixed concerns or wording that should be checked.
The rationale is ambiguous enough that a human reviewer should inspect the source row before official use.

glossary.definition: The proposal details as classified from the survey section, not a general view for or against housing.
A row-level label summarizing whether a written response is against, neutral, or in favor of the proposal as written.
A provisional keyword-assisted concern label inferred from classification rationale. One response can have multiple topic tags.
Rows prioritized for human review because confidence is medium or low, or because the response appears mixed or conditional.
A response that may support some goals while objecting to details such as parking, height, density, process, or safeguards.
The data summarizes written survey responses and is not a statistically weighted vote of all Narberth residents.

keyTakeaways: Across both analyzed sections, against-as-written classifications are the largest stance category.
Zone 4A has a higher against-as-written share than Zone 5B.
Topic tags are provisional and should be treated as exploration aids until human review.
discussionQuestions: Which proposal elements drive opposition: parking, height, density, process, affordability, or neighborhood character?
Which concerns are shared across both zones, and which are zone-specific?
Do mixed or conditional responses suggest amendments that could address resident concerns?
Which medium- or low-confidence classifications should be reviewed before official use?
What additional planning, affordability, infrastructure, or traffic evidence should be considered alongside resident sentiment?
limits: This is a classified readout of written survey responses, not a scientific referendum.
Representative cards summarize themes and do not display names or synthetic resident labels.
Topic tags are keyword-assisted from classification rationale and may undercount or overcount themes.
